title: Every poem is about you
takeaway: Love may be a bad bargain, but it's the only one worth making.
scene: This ghazal is in Urdu, not Punjabi. It's softer and more polished in tone. The poet admits that all his poetry comes from one source: his love and the pain of being apart.

original: مری سانسوں کو اس کے پیار کا کتنا سہارا ہے
مری آنکھوں سے اوجھل ہو مجھے یہ کب گوارا ہے
transliteration: Meri saanson ko us ke pyaar ka kitna sahaara hai
Meri aankhon se ojhal ho, mujhe yeh kab gawaara hai
translation: How much my very breathing leans on that love!
When could I ever bear for you to vanish from my sight?
couplets.story: His every breath depends on the Beloved's love. He can't stand the thought of them disappearing from view.

original: رکی نبضیں نہ کیونکر تیز ہوں بیمار ہجراں کی
میخانے نے ہی کیا نبضوں کو چلنے کا اشارہ ہے
transliteration: Ruki nabzen na kyunkar tez hon beemaar-e-hijraan ki
Maikhaane ne hi kiya nabzon ko chalne ka ishaara hai
translation: Why shouldn't the stopped pulse of one sick with separation race again?
It's the tavern itself that signalled the pulse to start beating.
couplets.story: He was so sick with missing the Beloved that his pulse had almost stopped. Then the 'tavern', the gathering of love, gave his heart the signal to start beating again.

original: شب ہجراں میں گزرے ہیں جو لمحے کرب کے اکثر
بظاہر میں نے ہنس ہنس کر وہ ہر لمحہ گزارا ہے
transliteration: Shab-e-hijraan mein guzre hain jo lamhe karb ke aksar
Bazaahir main ne hans hans kar woh har lamha guzaara hai
translation: All the moments of agony in the nights of separation,
on the outside I got through each one of them laughing.
couplets.story: Through every painful lonely night, he put on a smile. On the outside, he laughed his way through.

original: محبت اک شعلہ ہے بچا لو اس سے دامن کو
وہی سودا کیا میں نے سدا جس میں خسارہ ہے
transliteration: Mohabbat ik shola hai, bacha lo is se daaman ko
Wohi sauda kiya main ne sada jis mein khasaara hai
translation: Love is a flame; keep your clothes away from it.
I made exactly the deal that always ends in loss.
couplets.story: He warns that love is a fire, so keep your distance or you'll catch alight. Then he admits he did the opposite. He made the one deal that always loses.

original: میں ہوں فنکار تیرے حسن تک محدود سوچوں کا
ترے ہی شعر لکھ کر غزل کو بس نکھارا ہے
transliteration: Main hoon fankaar tere husn tak mehdood sochon ka
Tere hi sher likh kar ghazal ko bas nikhaara hai
translation: I'm an artist whose thoughts reach no further than your beauty;
I've polished the ghazal only by writing verses about you.
couplets.story: He calls himself an artist with only one subject: the Beloved's beauty. Every good poem he wrote was about them.

original: میرے ہر شعر میں ہجر و محبت کی کہانی ہے
صحیفہ پیار کا کس نے تیرے دل پر اتارا ہے
transliteration: Mere har sher mein hijr-o-mohabbat ki kahaani hai
Saheefa pyaar ka kis ne tere dil par utaara hai
translation: Every verse of mine tells a story of separation and love.
Who sent down a scripture of love upon your heart?
couplets.story: Every line he writes tells the same story of love and being apart. He wonders who sent down such a holy book of love onto the Beloved's heart.

original: ہوا جب بھی ہلاتی ہے میرے خستہ کواڑوں کو
گماں مجھ کو یہ ہوتا ہے مجھے تم نے پکارا ہے
transliteration: Hawa jab bhi hilaati hai mere khasta kiwaaron ko
Gumaan mujh ko yeh hota hai mujhe tum ne pukaara hai
translation: Whenever the wind rattles my worn-out doors,
I imagine it's you calling for me.
couplets.story: Every time the wind shakes his old, worn doors, he thinks it might be the Beloved knocking and calling his name.

original: میں خوشیاں اپنے حصے کی کروں تقسیم لوگوں میں
بتا گردش میں پھر احمدؔ کیوں تیرا ستارہ ہے
transliteration: Main khushiyaan apne hisse ki karoon taqseem logon mein
Bata gardish mein phir Ahmad kyun tera sitaara hai
translation: I share out my own portion of happiness among people;
so tell me, Ahmad, why is your star still caught in bad luck?
couplets.story: He gives away his own happiness to other people. So he asks himself why his luck is still so bad.

deeper: 'Who sent down a scripture of love upon your heart?' uses the word for revelation (sahifa, 'utaara'), the language used for holy books sent down by God. It's a bold way of saying love itself is a kind of sacred message. The image of the wind rattling the door and the poet thinking 'you are calling me' is the seeker's constant listening for God's call.
why: It shows the poet could write in Urdu as well as Punjabi, and its image of the wind at the door is simple and haunting.
prompt: Is there something you're always 'listening for', a call or a message you hope will come?
notes: This is the only ghazal in the book that is labelled as Urdu. The top lines of the photo are slightly blurry, but readable.
